data.title: Hypothalamic mTOR signaling regulates food intake
data.authors: Cota D; Proulx K; Smith KA; Kozma SC; Thomas G; Woods SC; Seeley RJ

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Rats (Long-Evans): fasting/refeeding, intracerebroventricular leucine, leptin and rapamycin; hypothalamic immunostaining and Western blot
data.finding: In rats, hypothalamic mTOR signalling (phosphorylated S6K1 and S6) changed with energy status in specific hypothalamic regions and was found in NPY and POMC neurons of the arcuate nucleus. Injecting leucine into the brain ventricles raised hypothalamic mTOR signalling and lowered food intake and body weight. Leptin also raised hypothalamic mTOR activity, and blocking mTOR with rapamycin in the brain blunted leptin's effect on reducing food intake. The authors proposed that hypothalamic mTOR acts as a fuel sensor linked to how much an animal eats. Boundary: rats, direct brain (intracerebroventricular) dosing, short-term food intake; drawn from the abstract only, so doses and effect sizes are not given here.
data.abstract_excerpt: The mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) protein is a serine-threonine kinase that regulates cell-cycle progression and growth by sensing changes in energy status. We demonstrated that mTOR signaling plays a role in the brain mechanisms that respond to nutrient availability, regulating energy balance. In the rat, mTOR signaling is controlled by energy status in specific regions of the hypothalamus and colocalizes with neuropeptide Y and proopiomelanocortin neurons in the arcuate nucleus.

extracted_findings.effect: Central leucine raised hypothalamic mTOR signalling and reduced food intake and body weight; mTOR inhibition blunted leptin anorexia
